column2: How does the pattern of visual loss localise a lesion relative to the chiasm?
column3: Monocular loss usually lies in one eye or the anterior visual pathway, whereas homonymous field loss lies behind the chiasm.

column2: How does a relative afferent pupillary defect appear, and what can it not distinguish on its own?
column3: Moving light to the worse eye makes both pupils constrict less or appear to dilate; it shows asymmetric severe retinal or optic-nerve dysfunction but cannot alone tell which.

column3: Keratitis can progress rapidly, especially in contact-lens wearers, and patching or casual steroid can accelerate destruction; urgent cultures and intensive organism-directed drops are needed instead.

column3: Orbital infection can cause optic-nerve compression, cavernous sinus thrombosis and intracranial spread, so urgent imaging and intravenous antibiotics are arranged.

column2: How long is a chemical eye injury irrigated, and why is alkali particularly damaging?
column3: Irrigation continues until ocular-surface pH remains neutral after stopping; alkali saponifies tissue and penetrates particularly rapidly, although acids can also injure deeply.
